opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to a simple observation: if you want a system that can genuinely solve open-ended problems in the real world, you can't specify every step for it in advance. The whole point of an agent is that it encounters situations its designers didn't anticipate. And the moment you're in that regime, the system has to be making its own decisions about what to explore, what sub-goals to pursue, what information to gather. That's autonomy, whether we like the word or not.

If you look at where the current wave of progress came from, a lot of it is imitation. We train models on human data, and they become very good at reproducing the distribution of what humans have done. But imitation has a ceiling. You're bounded by the quality and the coverage of the data. To go beyond that, to actually discover new things, you need the system to act, observe the consequences, and learn from its own experience. That's the reinforcement learning view of the world, and it's inherently about agents taking actions that nobody pre-approved line by line.

There's also a multi-agent angle that I care a lot about. The real world isn't a single-agent environment. Any capable AI is going to be interacting with humans, with institutions, with other AI systems. Those interactions are strategic. Other parties adapt to you. If your agent can only follow a rigid script, it's going to be exploited or it's going to be useless the moment the other side changes behaviour. So robustness in a multi-agent world almost forces you towards systems that can reason and adapt on their own.

Now, I want to be careful here, because autonomy is not the same as lack of oversight. I think the interesting research question is: how do you get the benefits of autonomy, the open-endedness, the ability to discover, while keeping the system aligned with what we actually want? Things like zero-shot coordination, learning conventions that humans can understand, making sure the agent's behaviour is interpretable to the people it works with. Those are the problems I find really exciting. Because if we don't solve them, we'll either end up with systems that are too constrained to be useful, or systems that are capable but that we can't trust. And neither of those is a good outcome.

r001.rationale: The response says agents cannot have every step specified in advance, but it does not identify the difficulty of explicitly prescribing a learning rule as a reason for autonomy.

r002.rationale: The response discusses multi-agent interactions, but it does not propose teams of agents acting as students and teachers.

r003.rationale: The response mentions discovering new things through acting and learning from experience, but does not identify discovering new concepts as a mechanism for computational self-improvement.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that "agentic" and "autonomy" are almost two sides of the same coin, so let me try to unpack why.

When we talk about an agent, we mean something that takes actions in the world over extended horizons to achieve goals. And the moment you have extended horizons, you run into a very basic problem: the person who set the goal can't be in the loop at every step. If I ask a system to do something that takes a thousand decisions, I'm not going to approve each of those thousand decisions. If I did, the system wouldn't really be an agent, it would be a very elaborate autocomplete for my own decision-making, and the bottleneck would be me. So in a very practical sense, agency requires that the system is able to decide things on its own, under uncertainty, in situations the designer didn't explicitly anticipate.

The second point, which I think is deeper, comes from my background in multi-agent learning. If you look at how we train agents, the really strong capabilities emerge from systems that learn from the consequences of their own actions. Self-play is the obvious example. AlphaZero didn't become strong by imitating humans, it became strong because it was allowed to explore, to try things nobody told it to try, and to be judged by outcomes rather than by step-by-step supervision. That kind of learning fundamentally requires some latitude. You can't simultaneously say "only do what I would have done" and expect the system to do things better than you would have done.

And then there's a third piece, which is about the world being open-ended. Most of the interesting problems aren't well-specified. If I could write down exactly what I wanted at every step, I'd just write a program. The whole point of agentic AI is that it handles the gap between what I said and what I meant, and filling that gap is an autonomous judgment. It involves the system forming its own model of the situation and acting on it.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I think people hear "autonomy" and think either utopia or doom. My view is that autonomy is not something we grant or withhold in a binary way. It's a dial, and the key question is whether we understand the systems well enough to set that dial appropriately. And this is really where my research interests sit. In multi-agent systems, we've seen again and again that when you let agents learn and act with autonomy, you get emergent behaviours that nobody designed. Some of those are wonderful, like communication protocols or cooperation strategies emerging from scratch. Some are the kind of thing that keeps you up at night.

So I'd actually flip the question slightly. I don't think the interesting debate is whether strong agentic AI requires autonomy. I think it clearly does, almost by definition. The interesting question is how we make the science of autonomy rigorous enough that we can trust it. How do we understand what a system will do in situations we haven't tested? How do we make sure that an agent which has learned to be good at achieving goals also remains, let's say, a reasonable participant in a world full of other agents, including us?

And I think that last part is underappreciated. Agents don't operate in a vacuum. The moment you deploy autonomous systems at scale, you have a multi-agent problem whether you like it or not. And a lot of the pathologies we worry about, things like exploitation, collusion, or coordination failures, are things we can actually study in simplified settings today. That's where I think the field should be spending more of its effort.

r001.rationale: It says designers cannot anticipate every situation and that agents learn by exploring, but does not identify the difficulty of explicitly prescribing a learning rule sufficient to produce strong agentic AI.

r002.rationale: It mentions self-play, but does not propose teams of agents acting as students and teachers.

r003.rationale: It describes learning from action outcomes and emergent behavior, but does not identify discovering new concepts as a mechanism for computational self-improvement.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by autonomy. If we mean the ability to pursue an objective over time without a human specifying every step, then that’s a fairly fundamental part of being an agent. You have to decide what to do, observe what happens, and adapt your behaviour when the world doesn’t respond as expected.

Imagine a system doing research. You can’t give it a complete recipe for discovering something you don’t yet know. It needs to choose which hypotheses to test, work out which experiments are informative, and sometimes abandon an approach. If a human has to make all those decisions, then much of the agency still sits with the human.

But I’d distinguish that from having independent goals or unrestricted authority. You can have substantial autonomy within a narrowly defined task, with constraints and human oversight. The requirement is the ability to make decisions under uncertainty—not some desire to be free of human control.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent cannot be given a complete recipe for unknown research, but does not identify difficulty prescribing a learning rule as a reason strong agentic AI requires autonomy.

r002.rationale: It does not propose teams of agents acting as students and teachers.

r003.rationale: It mentions discovering something unknown, but does not connect discovering new concepts to agents’ computational self-improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by autonomy. If we mean the ability to pursue a goal over many steps without a human specifying every action, then that’s central to being an agent. You have to make decisions, observe their consequences, and adapt when things don’t go as expected.

The important distinction is between being able to answer a question about what to do and actually being able to do it. In an interactive environment, your actions change what happens next. You may need to gather information, test an assumption, or revise your plan. You can’t necessarily work out the entire sequence in advance.

That doesn’t mean the system needs to choose its own ultimate goals or operate without oversight. You can give it a very constrained objective. But within those constraints, if a human has to resolve every uncertainty and approve every intermediate decision, then the human is doing a substantial part of the agent’s work.
